claims.text: The proposed intervention combines free-energy perturbation, umbrella sampling, and adaptive integration.
The framework can accurately compute solid and fluid phase free energies for complex multicomponent alloys.
The computed free energies retain vibrational, anharmonic, and electron-vibration contributions.
Umbrella potentials ensure adequate sampling of important transition pathways and anharmonic regions in both solid and fluid phases.
Adaptive biasing concentrates sampling in the most statistically relevant regions of configuration space.
Free-energy perturbation can bridge the relevant free-energy differences after adaptive umbrella sampling.
Reducing redundant sampling and emphasizing statistically relevant configurations will accelerate convergence of phase free energies.
The proposed method will reduce computational cost by at least one order of magnitude relative to explicit ab initio molecular-dynamics workflows.
For elemental and binary systems, the method will achieve free-energy accuracy competitive with TOR-TILD.
The method will avoid or overcome TOR-TILD's slowdown for multicomponent high-entropy alloys.
TOR-TILD slows substantially for multicomponent high-entropy systems.
Explicit ab initio molecular-dynamics free-energy calculations are accurate but computationally expensive.
Including full vibrational, anharmonic, and electron-vibration effects increases the expense of baseline phase-free-energy workflows.
The proposed method applies from pure elements and binary alloys through multicomponent high-entropy alloys near melting.
The method should be most effective near phase transitions in systems with moderate to high compositional complexity.
Exceptionally complex or strongly anharmonic free-energy landscapes may require additional calibration.
A greater than 5% discrepancy in key thermodynamic observables relative to explicit ab initio molecular dynamics is proposed as an unacceptable fidelity loss.
